notes: Nokia v InterDigital permission appeal; Jacob LJ on patent revocation motives and GSM essentiality declarations.

enrichment.short_title: Nokia v InterDigital: stay, 28 USC 1782 and GSM essentiality declaration
key_facts: InterDigital claimed essential GSM patents; Nokia sought revocation of three UK patents and declarations that they were not essential to GSM Release 4.
Nokia had a licence but commenced revocation proceedings partly to influence parallel ICC arbitration over royalties.
InterDigital applied to stay the action, restrain Nokia's 28 USC 1782 discovery in the US, and strike out pleadings inferring claim construction from essentiality assertions.
Pumfrey J refused the stay and injunction, allowed Nokia's amendment seeking a declaration of non-essentiality; InterDigital appealed.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Adjourned application for permission to appeal from Patents Court case management and pleading rulings in patent revocation and declaration proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Permission granted but appeal dismissed; InterDigital ordered to pay costs of the appeal, subject to immediate detailed assessment.
enrichment.ratio: Commercial motive to influence arbitration does not justify staying patent revocation; any person may challenge validity; a declaration whether patents are essential under ETSI standards is a clearly defined issue within the court's inherent jurisdiction even where the claimant holds a licence.
legal_issues: Whether revocation proceedings should be stayed pending ICC arbitration
Whether Nokia should be restrained from pursuing 28 USC 1782 applications
Whether pleadings inferring broad claim construction from essentiality claims should be struck out
Whether a declaration of non-essentiality was an appropriate remedy

notes: Family beneficial ownership trial; tenants in common finding upheld on multiple severance grounds.

enrichment.short_title: Barracks v Barracks: beneficial ownership of family home as tenants in common
key_facts: 45 Tentelow Lane was bought in 1986 by Ralph Barracks Senior and his mother Joanna Cummings, who provided more than half the purchase money.
A 1993 mortgage transfer declared the property held as tenants in common 50% to Mrs Cummings and 25% each to Mr Barracks and Alma Simmonds.
Mrs Cummings died in 2002 leaving her estate to her grandson Paul Barracks Junior; the father claimed survivorship under a joint tenancy.
The son sued to recover his grandmother's half share; Stanley Burnton QC's 2000 judgment and subsequent negotiations were relied on.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Chancery trial of a claim for declaration of beneficial ownership and an account following the grandmother's death.
enrichment.outcome: Claim upheld; beneficial interest held as tenants in common 50/50; father ordered to pay the claimant's costs.
enrichment.ratio: Standard survivorship wording in a transfer deed does not create a joint tenancy without a declaration of trust; a mortgage over half the equity, a counterclaim for sale, and later negotiations to buy out a half share each sever any joint tenancy, leaving a 50/50 tenants in common holding.
legal_issues: Whether the 1986 transfer created a joint tenancy or tenants in common
Whether the 1993 mortgage transaction severed any joint tenancy
Whether Mrs Cummings' 1995 counterclaim amounted to a section 36(2) notice to sever
Whether post-2000 negotiations mutually severed any remaining joint tenancy
linked_authorities: First National Security v Hegarty [1984] 1 All ER 139

notes: Meritless ILR judicial review dismissed; sham marriage, counterfeit stamp and wasted costs against solicitors.

enrichment.short_title: Lahcen v SoS: judicial review of removal after counterfeit ILR and 14-year rule refusal
key_facts: The claimant entered as a visitor in 1989; a 1992 marriage-based ILR application was refused after the marriage was found sham and subsistence ended.
He later relied on a counterfeit ILR stamp in an expired passport and was served administrative removal directions in July 2004.
A detailed November 2004 decision letter refused the 14-year concession and certified the Article 8 claim clearly unfounded.
After Bennett J adjourned for tape and forgery expert evidence, the claimant failed to pursue those steps or amend his claim and did not appear.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Substantive hearing of judicial review after adjournment for expert and tape evidence that was never obtained.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed on the merits and for non-attendance; claimant to pay costs on standard basis until 22 November 2004 and on indemnity basis thereafter; solicitors and Mr Otobo ordered to show cause on wasted costs.
enrichment.ratio: Where indefinite leave was never granted, removal after deception is lawful; deliberate evasion of immigration control excludes the 14-year policy; an unamended challenge to an superseding decision letter and failure to use an adjournment for expert evidence defeats the claim; Article 8 requires a truly exceptional case after Huang.
legal_issues: Lawfulness of removal after counterfeit ILR documentation
Whether the 14-year residence concession applied
Whether Article 8 was engaged by a relationship with a Czech EU national
Whether certification under section 94(2) was lawful
linked_authorities: R (Razgar) v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2004] UKHL 27
Huang v Secretary of State for the Home Department

notes: CCRC reference; unsafe 1986 convictions quashed for police conduct and identification evidence.

enrichment.short_title: R v Young: CCRC reference quashing 1986 criminal damage convictions
key_facts: Mr Young was convicted at a 1986 retrial of criminal damage to the Englands' home and car and possession of petrol bombs with intent.
The prosecution relied on Brenda England's identification and alleged confessions after a feud arising from divorce proceedings.

Police refused solicitor access for about 24 hours, failed to investigate Mr Young's complaint that interview notes were being fabricated, and used a windscreen-wiper theft to obtain a search warrant.
CCRC investigation produced photographs showing the claimed street-lamp identification line of sight was obstructed.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal (Criminal Division) reference by the Criminal Cases Review Commission; Crown did not resist allowing the appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; convictions quashed as unsafe; defendant's costs order for legal aid contribution and costs of first appeal.
enrichment.ratio: Cumulative police procedural failings including denial of solicitor access, failure to investigate fabrication complaints, a weak search-warrant basis, and fresh photographic evidence undermining critical identification can render long-standing convictions unsafe even if abuse of process would not have succeeded at trial.
legal_issues: Whether Brenda England's identification evidence was credible
Whether police denial of solicitor access breached the Judges' Rules
Whether failure to investigate fabrication complaints at the time vitiated the trial
Admissibility under section 23 of fresh photographic evidence unavailable to the defence

notes: Landmark Carillion v DML adjudication enforcement trial; Jackson J rejects all four challenges.

enrichment.short_title: Carillion v Devonport: enforcement of construction adjudicator's target cost decision

statutes_considered.title: Housing Grants, Construction and Regeneration Act 1996

key_facts: Carillion subcontracted 9 Dock upgrading works at Devonport Royal Dockyard under an Alliance Agreement with target cost and gainshare/painshare mechanics.
After £110 million paid, Carillion referred a £10.45 million dispute to adjudication; the adjudicator awarded further sums including bonus and fee.
DML challenged jurisdiction, natural justice, defects set-off reasoning and the power to award interest under paragraph 20(c) of the Scheme.
The trial proceeded within 22 days of issue with voluminous adjudication material before Jackson J.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Technology and Construction Court trial of parallel enforcement and validity challenges to an adjudicator's decision.
enrichment.outcome: All four challenges rejected; Carillion entitled to enforcement of the adjudicator's decision in full.
enrichment.ratio: An adjudicator answering the referred target cost question by preferring Carillion's October 2001 valuation does not exceed jurisdiction; declining to consider irrelevant MoD negotiation material or DML's alternative calculation is not breach of natural justice; a modest defects reduction without prior consultation is permissible; paragraph 20(c) of the Scheme confers a freestanding power to award interest.
legal_issues: Whether the adjudicator exceeded jurisdiction on target cost
Whether natural justice was breached by disregarding MoD settlement and alternative calculations
Whether defects allowance reasoning was inadequate or procedurally unfair
Whether paragraph 20(c) permits interest absent contractual provision

notes: Case stated appeal; Sedley LJ held lost CCTV did not make private hire prosecutions an abuse.

enrichment.short_title: Aylesbury Vale v Khan: abuse of process and lost CCTV in taxi prosecutions
key_facts: Aylesbury Vale prosecuted licensed private hire drivers for plying for hire without a hackney carriage licence.
Council officers approached cabs in the street but CCTV footage of the operation was negligently wiped.
Justices stayed the informations for abuse of process, finding the CCTV crucial to whether drivers knew fares were not pre-booked.
Defendants argued they may have believed officers were booked passengers.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court appeal by case stated from magistrates' decision staying informations as an abuse of process.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; answer 'no' to the stated question; proceedings remitted to continue before the justices.
enrichment.ratio: Negligent loss of corroborative CCTV does not amount to abuse of process where the prosecution can proceed on officer evidence and there was no deliberate suppression; section 78 PACE does not apply to the absence rather than introduction of evidence.
legal_issues: Whether lost CCTV made continuation an abuse of process
Applicability of section 78 PACE to missing evidence
Whether the prosecution was fundamentally flawed in evidence gathering
Whether delay alone justified a stay

notes: Hampstead Heath winter swimming JR; section 3 HSWA does not bar self-regulated pond use.

enrichment.short_title: Winter Swimming Club v Corporation of London: section 3 HSWA and Hampstead Heath pond

statutes_considered.title: Health and Safety at Work etc Act 1974

key_facts: The Hampstead Heath Winter Swimming Club sought permission to swim unsupervised in the Mixed Pond before official opening hours in winter.
The Corporation refused after counsel advised that granting permission could expose officers to prosecution under section 3 HSWA.
The HSE was joined but declined to participate, though its 2003 letter suggested risks could be controlled by agreement.
Stanley Burnton J held it appropriate to interpret section 3 despite the HSE's absence.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of the Corporation's refusal to permit self-regulated winter swimming, with HSE as interested party.
enrichment.outcome: Claim succeeded in principle; Corporation's July 2004 refusal based on erroneous section 3 advice was unlawful; declaration to be finalised on adjourned hearing.
enrichment.ratio: Where able adult swimmers voluntarily choose unsupervised swimming in a pond without hidden dangers, risks arise from their own decision not the employer's conduct of its undertaking, so granting permission does not expose the Corporation to section 3 criminal liability; Tomlinson principles inform the 'thereby' causation requirement.
legal_issues: Whether permitting self-regulated swimming exposes the Corporation to section 3 prosecution
Whether section 3 applies only to activities or also to static premises risks
Whether social value of swimming is relevant to 'reasonably practicable'
Propriety of interpreting a criminal statute without the HSE present
catchwords: Health and Safety at Work Act

Donoghue v Folkestone Properties Ltd [2003] EWCA Civ 231

notes: Listed building planning appeal dismissed; gatehouse link would destroy historic group integrity.

enrichment.short_title: Thompson v SoS: listed gatehouses linking extension appeal dismissed

statutes_considered.title: Planning (Listed Buildings and Conservation Areas) Act 1990

key_facts: Two Grade II listed gatehouses at the former Canon Hall Estate entrance were owned by Mr Thompson, who lived in the north lodge.
He applied to link the lodges with a stone extension incorporating the south lodge into his dwelling, raising gate walls and retaining closed gates.
A prior inspector's decision was quashed by Collins J for failing to allow explanation of apparent recent use of the south lodge.
Inspector Davison dismissed both planning and listed building appeals, finding serious harm to architectural and historic interest.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Section 288/63 challenge to a redetermined planning inspector's dismissal of planning and listed building consent appeals.
enrichment.outcome: Challenge dismissed; inspector's refusal upheld; claimant ordered to pay £3,660 costs.
enrichment.ratio: Linking paired gatehouses into a single dwelling destroys the historic entrance layout and architectural interest of facing pedimented doors; ancillary domestic uses may make a separated lodge viable without permitting harmful extension; an informed reading of 'eaves level' refers to the extension not the existing lodges.
legal_issues: Whether the south lodge had an economically viable ancillary use
Whether the appellant received a fair rehearing after Collins J's quashing
Whether the inspector misdescribed the proposed wall height
Application of PPG 15 presumption in favour of preservation

notes: Ethiopian Article 3 appeal; agreed remittal with credibility findings ring-fenced after Mlauzi.

enrichment.short_title: Ahmed v SoS: remittal of Ethiopian Article 3 appeal with ring-fenced findings
key_facts: The appellant, an Ethiopian national, entered the UK aged 16 in 1998 after mistreatment in Saudi Arabia and was taken into Westminster care.
An exceptional leave application made in 1999 was not decided for over four years before refusal and removal directions in 2003.
An adjudicator accepted her credibility and found Article 3 made out on psychiatric evidence of harm if returned.
The IAT overturned the decision without clearly identifying an error of law; after Mlauzi the Secretary of State conceded remittal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal permission and agreed disposal remitting to the AIT after IAT failed to identify a point of law.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; case remitted to AIT for rehearing; adjudicator's credibility and history findings ring-fenced; no order as to costs.
enrichment.ratio: Where the IAT did not identify the error of law giving it jurisdiction post-June 2003, remittal is appropriate; fairness permits ring-fencing an adjudicator's credibility findings while fresh country evidence on women's risk in Ethiopia is reconsidered for Article 3.
legal_issues: Whether the IAT identified a point of law for intervention
Correct Article 3 threshold after adjudicator's credibility findings
Whether four-year delay in deciding ELR affected the case
Effect of Mlauzi guidance on pending IAT appeals
linked_authorities: Mlauzi v Secretary of State for the Home Department (7 February 2005)

notes: Disability discrimination damages appeal; unfair dismissal does not break causation chain per Coudert Brothers.

enrichment.short_title: Beart v HM Prison Service: disability discrimination damages and Coudert Brothers
key_facts: Mrs Beart, a prison executive officer, went off with depression after mishandled part-time working inquiries and failure to redeploy her as Dr Harvey recommended.
She was dismissed in February 1999 after a flawed disciplinary investigation that withheld the private investigators' report.
Tribunals found disability discrimination and unfair dismissal; remedies included £22,000 personal injury and substantial future loss of earnings.
HM Prison Service appealed arguing unfair dismissal broke the chain of causation and capped loss at £12,000.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Second Court of Appeal hearing on remedies after liability upheld; appeal limited to loss of earnings causation.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; Prison Service cannot rely on its own unfair dismissal to limit disability discrimination damages.
enrichment.ratio: A tortfeasor cannot rely on its own subsequent wrongful act, including unfair dismissal, to break the chain of causation for earlier disability discrimination; Coudert Brothers applies whether the defendant or claimant raised the later wrong; material contribution to psychiatric injury supports continuing loss of earnings beyond dismissal.
legal_issues: Whether unfair dismissal breaks causation for disability discrimination loss of earnings
Applicability of Coudert Brothers to statutory discrimination torts
Whether Mrs Beart would have been dismissed even if relocated
Whether episodic depression prevented proof of continuing loss

Hotson v East Berkshire Area Health Authority [1987] AC 750
